title: Not All Toyotas Were the “EZ” Choice

body_markdown:
The Voluntary Export Restraint (VER) program of 1981 was intended to help American automakers during one of the most challenging times in their history by limiting the amount of Japanese vehicles coming into the U.S. The practice, a stark contrast to the free-market practices seen elsewhere in government at the time, would actually make things worse for Detroit’s Big Three.


When its effects were later studied, Stephen D. Cohen of American University[noted that VER caused no financial setbacks](https://nsarchive2.gwu.edu/japan/scohenwp.htm) to the established Japanese brands (Toyota, Nissan, Honda).


He went further, noting the Japanese “enjoyed windfall profits” which funded moves that “would make them an even greater competitive threat.” We saw this in the calculus behind[Nissan’s founding of the Infiniti brand](https://www.hagerty.com/media/automotive-history/infinitis-early-ads-wrote-checks-that-its-cars-never-cashed/#:~:text=Before%20that%2C%20though,under%20their%20skin%3F) and the[meteoric rise](https://www.hagerty.com/media/never-stop-driving/never-stop-driving-199-the-car-that-was-too-good/#:~:text=The%20full%20story,like%20a%20millionaire.%E2%80%9D) of Honda dealer markups during this period. The demand for Japanese cars was so strong that regardless of how many were coming in, almost every single one was flying out of showrooms—especially the affordable ones. The Tercel EZ, though, proved to be a case study in what the market would accept.


eBay | danel-8730


Toyota’s 1978 Tercel was the brand’s first-ever front-wheel-drive car, entering the market at the same time as the Dodge Omni/Plymouth Horizon, and one year before Ford’s Fiesta. Comparisons between the Tercel and its American competition are almost irrelevant because VER-fed scarcities ensured Toyota’s smaller dealership footprint had artificially inflated demand. (And likely more per-unit profit.)


But this isn’t an economic study, and VER ended in 1994. Toyota’s subcompact Tercel met its end just five years later. It was replaced by the Echo/Yaris (1999-2020), which were generally regarded as fantastic vehicles for their class, even though they didn’t have the staying power of their big brother, the Corolla. It appears that Toyota’s ability to please all consumers cannot overcome the fact that American consumers prefer larger vehicles. But there’s still more to the Tercel’s story.

The Tercel name refers to a male falcon. Earlier models leaned hard into the connection, with emblems and graphics worthy of the powerful bird of prey. There was a last hurrah in that regard, with a Black Hawk edition in the Tercel’s fifth generation. Toyota remained hawkish with every other car, truck, and SUV in the lineup, but the subcompact Tercel never seemed to flourish.


It possessed many of the qualities that buyers find appealing in Toyotas, including great fuel economy and well-built interiors. But the Tercel’s prevalence of carburetion through 1990 (Ford’s Escort had EFI in 1983), unpainted bumpers, four-speed manual transmissions, and cabins light on accoutrements ensured the Tercel wasn’t as appealing as a Civic or Corolla. It wasn’t the best value in its highly price-sensitive market, either. Base prices were around $4000 in the early 1980s and bumped up to $5848 for the base EZ Tercel in 1988.


That was an uncomfortable space, as American cars ranging from the 1980 Pinto to the 1989 Geo Metro often sold for much less, as Detroit automakers loved to throw cash on the hood to move their mass-produced, non-VER-constrained metal. Above the Tercel EZ were cars like the Honda Civic, Nissan Sentra, Ford Escort, and Chevrolet Cavalier. While Honda was famously stingy on incentives, the others had numerous periods of heavy discounting that made them a superior buy for would-be Tercel owners.


The Tercel LE presented in the above *Motorweek* video stickers at a seemingly modest $9478. But it was only a matter of time before that subcompact value proposition was cross-shopped with value-oriented versions of compact vehicles like the 1993 Chevrolet Cavalier VL, which started at a shockingly low $8600. The VL likely kissed the $8K mark with periodic factory incentives and loss-leader pricing at dealerships, and such tactics might be another reason why the subcompact Tercel never took off with the American consumer. *(We aren’t even considering the added markup from Toyota’s two regional distributors, known for hiking up prices with ill-fitting floor mats and the cheapest alloy wheels on the market.)*


Tercel sales peaked in 1988, with over 104,000 units sold. That’s even 2000 more units than the all-new 1990 model, now in its fourth generation and losing sales steam every subsequent year. By its fifth generation (1994), the Tercel only mustered around 88,000 units. It tapered off to 31,489 units by 1997, and a forlorn 46 units changed hands in 1999.


This is a shocking swing and a miss for an automaker known for home runs in darn near every segment it occupies. Cars like the Cavalier VL and Geo Metro aside, we are ignoring the elephant in the room. Reviews of the era didn’t know discuss why new Tercels met with less and less fanfare in new car showrooms.


What should have been an honest Toyota product with all its associated value and reliability was actually a bit of a fragile teacup. While my local mechanic at the time didn’t partake in the “ter-smell” or “turd-cell” name-calling, he told customers to avoid them. Years of tuning issues with carburetors in an era of fuel injection were one thing, but oil consumption and blowing head gaskets were another. Apparently their valve guides weren’t up to spec for oil control.


Oil can be refilled as needed, but budget-destroying head gasket failures were not. The latter isn’t unique to this car, as everything from Toyota’s Supra to Ford’s ubiquitous[3.8-liter Essex V-6](https://www.hagerty.com/media/video/1990-was-fords-year-of-the-essex-machine/) utilized the tragic combination of an iron block, aluminum heads, and inadequate gasket technology to earn a place of infamy in automotive history. While a blown gasket on a Supra likely met with modest disappointment with its well-heeled buyers, it’s a death sentence for those owning a depreciated Tercel.


1996 Toyota Tercel Black Hawk


Toyota


This is where reputation meets reality. While Toyotas are celebrated for their quality and durability, back then, its inflated price tags didn’t jive with what the Tercel offered, and what it put many a customer through after its warranty expired. Subcompact cars are often cheerful and affordable, but Toyota’s Tercel was a tad subdued and somewhat expensive.


While plenty of cars in the Tercel’s class had an iron block with an aluminum head, they weren’t riding the coattails of a brand known for premium prices in exchange for more value. It’s fair to say that most subcompact cars are throwaway appliances in America, but it’s unfair to pay more for that privilege.
